However, the study found significant data limitations, including a lack of detailed information on existing refueling depot locations, location-specific biofuel availability, and sufficient granularity in commodity and location data (like specific chemicals at precise locations). These limitations pose challenges for developing a comprehensive alternative fuel transition strategy, and they warrant additional research. 65 7.9 SCALE-UP ANALYSIS The scale-up analysis evaluated the potential benefits and tradeoffs of scaling up biofuel use in the U.S. rail sector. The analysis used the Bioeconomy AGE model, which integrates data about alternative fuel production, rail fuel demand, and lifecycle assessments. Scaling up biofuel use in the U.S. rail sector—particularly RD and BD, which are derived mainly from soybeans and waste feedstocks—has strong potential to meet or exceed rail diesel demand by 2035. RD-HEFA is the dominant near-term pathway, while woody and herbaceous biomass offer longer-term opportunities. This transition could reduce CO e emissions by around 69–77% compared to 2 conventional diesel, although SO , particulate matter and NO emissions may increase in some X X cases. However, increased water consumption is a significant environmental tradeoff due to the high water intensity of biofuel production, especially from soybean-based pathways. Regional variations in biofuel supply and demand, feedstock availability, and infrastructure logistics will influence cost and adoption feasibility, highlighting the need for more detailed analysis at a granular level to fully assess biofuel implementation feasibility on specific rail routes. There is also a need for further research to optimize water consumption in biomass conversion processes due to the increased water use associated with scaling up biofuel production. 66 REFERENCES AAR (Association of American Railroads), 2025, "Resources." https://www.aar.org/resources/.
